article_title: A Formative Study of Brief Affective Text as a Complement to Wearable Sensing for Longitudinal Student Health Monitoring
citation: Tamunotonye Harry, Johanna Hidalgo, Matthew Price, Yuanyuan Feng, Kathryn Stanton, Connie Tompkins, Peter Sheridan Dodds, Mikaela Irene Fudolig, Laura Bloomfield, and Christopher Danforth. 2026. A Formative Study of Brief Affective Text as a Complement to Wearable Sensing for Longitudinal Student Health Monitoring. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. 10, 4, Article 219 (December 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14360
title: Use ultra-brief affective prompts to enrich the psychological interpretability of passive physiological data at minimal participant burden
description: The article's design guidance is that a single open-ended affective question, answered in the participant's own words, can complement passive wearable sensing by supplying psychological context the sensors cannot recover. Responses were extremely short — the median was three words — yet still associated with within-person variation in sleep and activity outcomes. The article concludes that "ultra-brief affective prompts enrich the psychological interpretability of passive physiological data at minimal burden", positioning this as a lightweight alternative to infrastructure-intensive sensor-language models.
requirements: A single open-ended concern prompt integrated into an existing study protocol (here, a bimonthly ecological momentary assessment delivered via a study mobile application), paired with concurrent wearable outcome data aggregated over the same two-week window.
constraints: The concern prompt is negatively valenced by construction, selectively surfacing worry and distress; the authors state findings should be read within that scope.
The bimonthly interval is a design constraint representing a middle point in the burden-versus-sensitivity tradeoff, not an optimum established by the study.
Associations are formative and exploratory; none survived correction for multiple comparisons.
target_learners: first-year university students in longitudinal health monitoring studies
examples: Participants in the LEMURS study responded bimonthly to the prompt 'Of all the things that have happened in the last 2 weeks, what concerns you the most?', producing 3,073 concern-present responses with a median length of three words alongside continuous Oura ring wear.
key_sources: Tamunotonye Harry, Johanna Hidalgo, Matthew Price, Yuanyuan Feng, Kathryn Stanton, Connie Tompkins, Peter Sheridan Dodds, Mikaela Irene Fudolig, Laura Bloomfield, and Christopher Danforth. 2026. A Formative Study of Brief Affective Text as a Complement to Wearable Sensing for Longitudinal Student Health Monitoring. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. 10, 4, Article 219 (December 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14360

article_title: Learning and navigating digitally rendered haptic spatial layouts
citation: Ruxandra I. Tivadar, Benedetta Franceschiello, Astrid Minier and Micah M. Murray. (2023). Learning and navigating digitally rendered haptic spatial layouts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00208-4
title: Ultrasonic digital haptics tablet rendering floor plans and trajectories as friction-reduction textures
description: A tablet-based surface haptic display in which "the touchscreen of a tablet device monitors the position of the fingertip" and "localised piezoelectric actuators, in turn, vibrate at ultrasonic frequencies to dynamically change the perceived friction at the fingertip and thus give the impression of texture". In the study it rendered an apartment floor plan with four textures (walls, furniture obstacles, areas outside, and the trajectory), using square-wave ultrasonic signals for sharp sensations and a sinusoidal signal for the trajectory. It served as the sole learning medium for the 2D layout before physical reconstruction and blindfolded navigation.
requirements: Users require familiarisation and training to discriminate the haptic textures and learn exploration strategies (lateral finger sweeps) before the layout can be learned.
constraints: The haptic maps used only the two ultrasonic wave shapes provided natively in the device's Haptic Texture Library Creation Tool, limiting the textures to those the tool provides.
target_learners: sighted blindfolded adults learning unfamiliar spatial layouts; proposed for visually impaired and blind populations in rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: spatial layout learning, cognitive map formation, and navigation of real-world trajectories
examples: In the study, 25 blindfolded participants learned the apartment layout solely from the tablet's haptic rendering, reconstructed it with LEGO bricks, and navigated trained and untrained trajectories in the real space.
key_sources: Ruxandra I. Tivadar, Benedetta Franceschiello, Astrid Minier and Micah M. Murray. (2023). Learning and navigating digitally rendered haptic spatial layouts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00208-4

article_title: Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities
citation: Sabirova, E. G., Zakirova, V. G. & Masalimova, A. R. (2016). Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 505-514.
title: Four units of universal learning activities (personal, regulative, cognitive, communicative) mapped onto junior pupils' research skills
description: The article organizes junior pupils' research skills through the Russian second-generation standards' four units of universal learning activities: "personal, regulative (also including self-regulation), cognitive, communicative". Each unit is correlated with specific research skills: the personal unit with seeing the problem, proposing hypotheses and representing results; the regulative unit with purpose formation, planning, prognostication, correction and estimation; the cognitive unit with hypothesizing, questioning, classifying, structuring material and proving ideas; and the communicative unit with questioning, discourse, proving and representing results. The study used this mapping to specify the content of research skills in interconnection with universal learning activities.
requirements: Purposeful formation of research skills during lessons, as the Russian standards require, so the interrelations can be developed rather than left to spontaneous formation
constraints: The article states the interrelations are conditional and defined by the present stage, with links that correct needed action content at every age period of junior pupils
target_learning_goals: research skills such as seeing problems, proposing hypotheses, questioning, classifying, structuring material, discourse, proving ideas, and representing results
examples: The article lists subject-embedded tasks for each skill, e.g. mathematics tasks for seeing the problem such as finding text with excessive or insufficient content, and environment tasks for hypothesizing such as prognosticating weather phenomena.
key_sources: Sabirova, E. G., Zakirova, V. G. & Masalimova, A. R. (2016). Development of Junior Pupils Research Skills in Interrelation with Universal Learning Activities. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 505-514. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094583

article_title: The application of CBL and mind mapping combined with Mini-CEX teaching mode in the cultivation of clinical competence of ultrasound residents.
citation: Liu Rong, Li Lei, Zhou Ying, Xiong Lu. (2025). The application of CBL and mind mapping combined with Mini-CEX teaching mode in the cultivation of clinical competence of ultrasound residents. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0327739
title: Ultrasound-adapted Mini-CEX assessing six competency areas with immediate feedback
description: An improved Mini Clinical Evaluation Exercise tailored to ultrasound practice, used both as an evaluation instrument and as a feedback mechanism during training. It assesses residents during routine ultrasound procedures across six areas: "medical history taking, ultrasound examination, doctor-patient communication, clinical reasoning, organizational efficiency, and overall performance", aligned with ACGME core competencies. Scores of 1–3 are deemed insufficient, 4–6 qualified, and 7–9 excellent. The authors state it provides "immediate feedback and guidance" by monitoring interactions with patients and colleagues and adherence to standard protocols.
requirements: Requires instructors who directly observe residents during ultrasound examinations and deliver feedback after each evaluation
constraints: The article notes the Mini-CEX assessment may be subject to subjective biases from instructors, and reviewers noted the modified rubric's modification and pilot-testing process was not documented
target_learners: ultrasound residents and general practitioners in standardized residency training
target_learning_goals: clinical competence in ultrasound, including communication, clinical reasoning and procedural skills
examples: Used at three time points (admission, two weeks, four weeks) to track experimental-group residents' progress during the 4-week training
key_sources: Liu Rong, Li Lei, Zhou Ying, Xiong Lu. (2025). The application of CBL and mind mapping combined with Mini-CEX teaching mode in the cultivation of clinical competence of ultrasound residents. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0327739

article_title: Intelligence in Context: A Context-specific Mindset Measure Better Predicts Outcomes for Science and Math Undergraduates.
citation: Limeri, Lisa B. (2025). Intelligence in Context: A Context-specific Mindset Measure Better Predicts Outcomes for Science and Math Undergraduates. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 24(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-09-0229
title: ULTrA Survey: a context-specific mindset measure for science and math undergraduates
description: The Undergraduate Lay Theories of Abilities (ULTrA) Survey is a mindset measure developed specifically for undergraduate science and math students through an iterative four-stage development process integrating quantitative and qualitative data. "The ULTrA Survey consists of 25 items measuring five factors (5 items each): growth mindset, fixed mindset, universal belief, nonuniversal belief, and brilliance belief." Its items use ability terms undergraduates interpret consistently (analyzing information, applying knowledge, ability to learn, intellectual ability) instead of the word intelligence, and measurement invariance analyses indicated it functions equivalently across disciplines, institution types, and personal characteristics.
requirements: Developed and validated for the undergraduate science and math context; validity evidence should be re-examined when used in other samples or contexts
constraints: The fixed factor is 2 items longer than the 3-item original mindset measure, so it may not suit researchers constrained in survey length or needing to minimize participant burden
Developed to be specific to undergraduate math and science educational contexts
target_learning_goals: Measurement of mindset beliefs (fixed, growth, universality, brilliance) in undergraduate science and math education research
examples: In this study, the 5-item fixed factor of the ULTrA was compared against the 3-item original mindset measure in SEMs predicting seven psychosocial and academic outcomes
key_sources: Limeri, Lisa B. (2025). Intelligence in Context: A Context-specific Mindset Measure Better Predicts Outcomes for Science and Math Undergraduates. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 24(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.24-09-0229

article_title: AI-enhanced guidance demonstrated improvement in novices' Apical-4-chamber and Apical-5-chamber views.
citation: Karni Ofri, Shitrit Itamar Ben, Perlin Amit, Jedwab Roni, Wacht Oren, Fuchs Lior. (2025). AI-enhanced guidance demonstrated improvement in novices' Apical-4-chamber and Apical-5-chamber views. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06905-5
title: UltraSight real-time AI guidance software for cardiac ultrasound probe navigation and image quality
description: UltraSight's FDA-approved AI software, used with a Philips Lumify probe on an Android tablet, provides on-screen instructions guiding probe tilting, rocking, rotation and sliding, plus a real-time quality bar indicator. The article states it "provides on-screen instructions to guide the user on adjusting the US probe" and "conducts a real-time analysis of the cardiac US image, reflected in the quality bar indicator". It was the sole difference between the trial's two training groups.
requirements: Requires a compatible Philips Lumify probe and Android-operated tablet device with the pre-installed software
constraints: The article notes most AI-based tools necessitate the presence of a skilled POCUS operator during the tool's operation, and novices may initially find on-screen instructions challenging to navigate
examples: In the trial, the intervention group received a brief introduction to the software's navigation guidance and quality indicator features, then used it during training and testing while the control group used the same device without AI support
key_sources: Karni Ofri, Shitrit Itamar Ben, Perlin Amit, Jedwab Roni, Wacht Oren, Fuchs Lior. (2025). AI-enhanced guidance demonstrated improvement in novices' Apical-4-chamber and Apical-5-chamber views. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06905-5

article_title: The pivot to online teaching: an opportunity to create effective problem-based learning environments for dietetic education.
citation: Griffin A. (2025). The pivot to online teaching: an opportunity to create effective problem‐based learning environments for dietetic education. J Hum Nutr Diet. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.13378
title: Interdisciplinary online PBL 'Health Technology' project pairing dietetic and engineering students at University of Limerick
description: A four-stage online PBL task conducted during COVID-19 in which "students to work in small interdisciplinary teams to design a solution to the authentic problem of conducting height assessment remotely using the sensors and instrumentation available on their smartphones". Teams of one dietetic student with one to two engineering students used MS Teams channels, recorded 1-min video proposals, used Miro collaboration boards, undertook self-directed learning (LabVIEW development for engineers, nutrition assessment understanding for dietitians), and submitted technical reports and reflections with 3-min prerecorded presentations marked jointly by both module leads. Modules were CT6061 (15 first-year graduate-entry dietetic students) and ET4305 (23 third-year engineering students), each 12 weeks, 6 ECTS.
requirements: Educators adopting a facilitator role to guide the PBL process
Module leads timing each team's contribution to ensure equitable discussion time
constraints: Conducted in an online environment necessitated by COVID-19
examples: The article reports the project helped mitigate the sense of isolation common in online learning environments, citing Johnson and Griffin (2024)
key_sources: Griffin A. (2025). The pivot to online teaching: an opportunity to create effective problem‐based learning environments for dietetic education. J Hum Nutr Diet. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.13378

article_title: Teaching medical students ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of synthetic cysts: effect of a formalin-embalmed cadaver simulation model.
citation: Stathas SpiroAnthony, Baribeau Vincent, Kutch Maximillian, Zapata Isain, Thomson Andrew, Mason Nena Lundgreen. (2024). Teaching medical students ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of synthetic cysts: effect of a formalin-embalmed cadaver simulation model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05907-z
title: Use ultrasound-trained peers and anatomy faculty as instructors to expand access to ultrasound-guided procedural training
description: Because instructor type did not affect any measured outcome, the article recommends that ultrasound-trained peers and anatomy faculty be used alongside physicians to deliver this training. It argues this "may help address the demand for US educators" given the reported shortage of ultrasound instructors, and that the non-contributory role of instructor type underscores how accessible such cadaveric training programs are for medical schools. Standardized training rubrics are the stated condition for this multi-instructor delivery model.
requirements: Instructors with prior ultrasound teaching experience
Standardized training rubrics used during training sessions
constraints: The finding comes from a single-center study of 30 novices with essentially no prior ultrasound experience; the article calls for a power analysis in future studies
examples: The study assigned participants to a second-year medical student with 3 years' teaching experience, a clinical anatomist with 9 years' experience, or an emergency medicine physician with 3 years' experience, all using a common teaching rubric
key_sources: Stathas SpiroAnthony, Baribeau Vincent, Kutch Maximillian, Zapata Isain, Thomson Andrew, Mason Nena Lundgreen. (2024). Teaching medical students ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of synthetic cysts: effect of a formalin-embalmed cadaver simulation model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05907-z

article_title: Undergraduate Lay Theories of Abilities: Mindset, universality, and brilliance beliefs uniquely predict undergraduate educational outcomes.
citation: Limeri Lisa B., Carter Nathan T., Lyra Franchesca, Martin Joel, Mastronardo Halle, Patel Jay, Dolan Erin L. (2023). Undergraduate Lay Theories of Abilities: Mindset, universality, and brilliance beliefs uniquely predict undergraduate educational outcomes. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.22-12-0250
title: ULTrA Survey: a 25-item short-form measure of undergraduate lay theories of abilities
description: The Undergraduate Lay Theories of Abilities (ULTrA) survey measures science and math undergraduates' mindset, universality, and brilliance beliefs. Its recommended short form contains "five items for each factor (25 total)" covering growth mindset, fixed mindset, brilliance belief, universal belief, and nonuniversal belief, selected by item response theory analyses to maximize item difficulty range, discrimination, and test information while covering each construct's full conceptual range. Items use STEM-contextualized wording (e.g., referencing analyzing information, applying knowledge, and learning) chosen because undergraduates interpret the generic term intelligence unreliably. Validity evidence was collected across four phases following the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing framework.
requirements: Administered with the printed prompt asking students to indicate agreement with statements about STEM abilities, with no correct answers
constraints: Developed for undergraduate science and math contexts; the article notes context-generic mindset items create validity issues in undergraduate education
The article notes men and 2-yr institution students were underrepresented in the phase-3 sample
target_learners: Undergraduate science and math students in introductory Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Math courses
target_learning_goals: Measuring students' beliefs about the improvability of intelligence, the distribution of potential for excellence, and whether success requires innate brilliance
examples: The recommended short form includes items such as "Excelling in STEM requires natural talent." for brilliance and "With enough hard work, anyone could become as good at analyzing information as highly successful STEM professionals." for universal belief
key_sources: Limeri Lisa B., Carter Nathan T., Lyra Franchesca, Martin Joel, Mastronardo Halle, Patel Jay, Dolan Erin L. (2023). Undergraduate Lay Theories of Abilities: Mindset, universality, and brilliance beliefs uniquely predict undergraduate educational outcomes. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.22-12-0250
